label: win (both exams, same-budget control)
result: Against the same networks under the standard search at the same budget: on unseen boards it solved 186 vs 182 and improved the move count on 31 of 32 differing shared solves (fluke chance ~1 in 60 million); on the standard exam it solved 231 of 232 with 30/0 move wins and cut extra-moves-vs-perfect from 1.42 to 1.01 -- BELOW the pure-subgoal language's proven floor of 1.17, the first ceiling break of the project. In absolute terms on the 137 unseen puzzles where perfect play is known (needing 8.71 moves on average): the hybrid solves 135 and uses +1.67 moves over perfect (56% solved perfectly), vs +1.94 for the same nets without slides, +2.9-3.3 for the A* line, +4.84 for the supervised backward planner; the forward planner is near-perfect when it solves (+0.12) but solves only 101. Caveat: the forward baseline is the original network; a carefully re-tuned forward planner would likely solve a few more puzzles and could narrow this gap measurement slightly -- at the size where re-tuning was tried (smaller boards, 8 robots), it gained 8 hard puzzles out of 184 (main FINDINGS 24).
conclusion: Adopted for inference: letting the planner make one ordinary robot move before subgoal planning is the first change to break the subgoal language ceiling, and it wins on every exam against its same-budget control. Next (wave 4): teach the networks about slides during training, and try two-slide roots.
note: Search-only change (no training); stochasticity is the search rng only. Gates: unseen moves 31/1 p=1.5e-8; graded moves 30/0 p=1.9e-9.
